newsitem.title: USA: Dollar/yen starts higher in U.S., nears 116 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen starts higher in U.S., nears 116 yen.

text.p: The dollar opened solidly higher versus the yen, bolstered by remarks from a Japanese financial official and news that the London branch of a major bank in Japan suffered huge losses from derivatives trading, currency experts said.
Jiji Press quoted Japanese Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa as saying neither the yen's excessive strength or excessive weakness was desirable.
Furthermore, Reuters reported that Ogawa said concerns since the beginning of April over an excessively weak yen had completely disappeared.
Reuters also quoted Ogawa as saying it was important to the Japanese economy for exchange rates to be stable.
The dollar-yen exchange rate has been anything but stable recently. Earlier in the week, an embattled greenback tumbled to a five-month low of 111.98 yen.

"Since the yen has now been strengthening ferociously, when they call for market stability, the assumption is they don't want it to strengthen any more and they threaten to limit yen strength," said Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch.
The dollar opened at 115.85/95 yen, sharply higher than 114.32/37 at Wednesday's close.
The Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ) reported on Thursday that its London branch had made a 10 billion yen ($86.9 million) loss from derivatives trading as of April 1.
In March, Japan's top bank, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, admitted its New York arm had incurred losses of around $50 million in instruments such as U.S. interest rate swaps.
"We have to anticipate there are going to be steady reports of banking sector losses for another 18 months or so," Harris said.
"When they happen, there is some concern that that lengthens the time during which the BOJ (Bank of Japan) has to leave rates low because that helps banks avoid collapse," Harris added.

The BOJ has kept its official discount rate at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995. Ogawa also said on Thursday that the Japanese Ministry of Finance agrees with the BOJ's low interest rate policy.
Although dollar/yen scored solid gains on Thursday, a trader at the New York branch of a Japanese bank said the dollar will have a tough time breaking above 116.50 yen.
The trader cited offers to sell dollars for yen from Japanese exporters and investors at 116.50.
Elsewhere, the dollar opened at 1.6930/35 marks, marginally higher than 1.6928/33 marks at the prior close. Shortly after the opening, the greenback turned lower.
Traders linked dollar weakness versus the mark to gains in the mark/yen cross.
The German currency traded around 68.39/41 yen shortly after the opening, up from about 68.31/34 yen in very early dealings.
Dollar/mark is just being used as a cross vehicle for movements in mark/yen, said Steven Walker, a senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York.
Walker pegged support for the dollar around 1.6875 marks. In other trading, the dollar opened at 1.4108/18 Swiss francs, up from 1.4075/85 francs at the previous close.
Sterling fell to $1.6380/90 from $1.6450/60.
The dollar opened at Canadian $1.3708/13, up from C$1.3677/82.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7821/26, down from $0.7866/71. ((Donna Sells, 212-859-1668))
